name: Sokoto Caliphate
summary: A Sunni Muslim caliphate founded by Usman dan Fodio in a jihad against the Hausa kingdoms. By 1837 it was the most populous state in West Africa, until British, French and German conquest in 1903.

location.value: Northern Nigeria and parts of Niger, Cameroon and Burkina Faso.

terrain.value: Savannah and the Sahel south of the Sahara.

climate.value: Hot, with a long dry season and a short rainy season.

resources.value: Farmland, cotton and indigo, cattle, and trade.

population.value: Perhaps 10–20 million people by the mid-19th century, one of Africa’s largest states.

urbanisation.value: Kano, Sokoto and Zaria were major cities.

disease.value: Unknown in detail; the explorer Hugh Clapperton died near Sokoto in 1827.

migration.value: Fulani pastoralists and scholars moved across the region.

economicBase.value: Farming, textiles (Kano cloth), and trade; slave labour on plantations.

tradeRoutes.value: Trans-Saharan trade and routes south to the coast.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; Kano was a rich textile centre.

moneyAndTax.value: Cowries; Islamic taxes and tribute from emirates.

inequality.value: Fulani rulers and scholars over Hausa farmers and many slaves.

governmentType.value: A caliphate made of many emirates under the Sultan of Sokoto.

keyRulers.value: Usman dan Fodio (founder), Muhammad Bello, Nana Asma’u (scholar and poet).

succession.value: Caliphs were chosen from among the descendants of Usman dan Fodio.

institutions.value: Emirs governed provinces under Islamic law.

stability.value: Fairly stable for a century, held together by Islam and loyalty to the caliph.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalries between emirates and revolts by subject peoples.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry and infantry; few modern guns compared with the British.

majorWars.value: The Fulani War (1804–1808) against the Hausa kingdoms.

territoryChange.value: Expanded across northern Nigeria and into Niger and Cameroon by 1837.

scienceEducation.value: Islamic scholarship and many books in Arabic and Fulfulde.

openness.value: A reform movement that encouraged literacy and learning, including for women (Nana Asma’u).

communicationTransport.value: Horses and donkeys; caravan routes; messengers carrying letters in Arabic.

religion.value: Sunni Islam, with the Qadiriyya Sufi order.

languageWriting.value: Arabic, Fulfulde and Hausa in Ajami script.

artsArchitecture.value: Mosques and palaces in mud brick; the Kano dye pits.

socialStructure.value: A Fulani ruling elite, Hausa commoners and many slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Islam united the different peoples of the caliphate.

dailyLife.value: Mud-walled compounds; millet, sorghum and dairy from Fulani herds.

neighbours.value: Bornu, Oyo, Borgu, later the British and French.

ideasReligions.value: Islamic reform and learning spread through the region.

colonisation.value: Conquered by Britain, France and Germany in 1903.

riseSignals.value: Usman dan Fodio’s jihad (1804–1808) against the Hausa kingdoms.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Sokoto Caliphate (checked 6 Nov 2026); Last, The Sokoto Caliphate (1967)

peakPeriod.value: By 1837 the most populous state in West Africa.

declineSignals.value: European colonial expansion at the end of the 19th century.

outcome.value: Annexed into Northern Nigeria and neighbouring colonies; the Sultan of Sokoto remains a religious leader.

sources.value: Arabic writings of the jihad leaders. Checked against Wikipedia (“Sokoto Caliphate”).

overallCertainty.value: Good. Many Arabic writings of its leaders survive.

knownFor.label: Usman dan Fodio
knownFor.note: Scholar and founder of the caliphate.

knownFor.label: Nana Asma’u
knownFor.note: A poet and teacher who educated women.

knownFor.label: Kano cloth
knownFor.note: Indigo-dyed cloth traded across West Africa.
